what_its_for: Gentamicin is an antibiotic used to fight serious bacterial infections. It can treat infections of the blood, lungs, skin, bones, joints, urinary tract, and abdomen. It is also available as eye drops or ointment to treat eye infections. It only works against bacterial infections and will not treat colds, flu, or other viral illnesses.
how_to_take: Gentamicin given by injection or IV will be prepared and given to you by a nurse or doctor in a clinic or hospital. If you are using gentamicin eye drops: tilt your head back, pull your lower eyelid down to form a small pocket, and place the prescribed number of drops into the pocket. Close your eye gently for 1 to 2 minutes. Do not let the dropper tip touch your eye or any surface. If using the eye ointment, apply a small ribbon of ointment inside your lower eyelid. Wash your hands before and after each use.
dosing: Your dose will be determined by your doctor based on your weight, kidney function, and the type of infection you have. For injections or IV: doses are typically given every 8 to 24 hours depending on your specific situation. For eye drops: usually 1 to 2 drops in the affected eye every 4 to 8 hours, or as directed by your doctor. For eye ointment: usually applied 2 to 3 times daily, or as directed. Always follow your doctor's exact instructions and complete the full course of treatment even if you feel better.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take or use it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not double up on doses to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist for guidance.
storage: Store gentamicin eye drops and ointment at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep the bottle or tube tightly closed when not in use. Do not freeze. Keep out of reach of children. Discard eye drops or ointment after the number of days recommended by your pharmacist, even if some medication is left. Injectable gentamicin will be stored and handled by your healthcare team.
what_to_avoid: Avoid touching the tip of the eye drop bottle or ointment tube to your eye, fingers, or any other surface to prevent contamination. Do not wear contact lenses while being treated for an eye infection unless your doctor says it is okay. Tell your doctor about all other medications you take, especially other antibiotics, diuretics (water pills like furosemide), or pain relievers like ibuprofen, as these can increase the risk of kidney or hearing problems when combined with gentamicin. Avoid driving or operating heavy machinery if your vision is temporarily blurry after using eye drops or ointment.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away if you experience any of the following: ringing, buzzing, or roaring in your ears; hearing loss or changes in hearing; dizziness, spinning sensation, or trouble with balance; decreased urination or dark-colored urine (signs of kidney problems); numbness, tingling, or muscle twitching; severe skin rash or itching; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; or if your eye symptoms worsen or do not improve within a few days. These could be signs of serious side effects that need immediate attention.
when_it_works: For eye infections, you may start to notice improvement within 2 to 3 days of starting treatment. For serious infections treated by injection or IV, improvement is often seen within 48 to 72 hours. It is very important to finish the entire course of treatment even if you feel better sooner, to make sure the infection is completely cleared and to prevent antibiotic resistance.
special_populations: Older adults and people with kidney disease are at higher risk for hearing loss and kidney damage and will need extra monitoring and possible dose adjustments. Pregnant or breastfeeding women should discuss risks with their doctor before using gentamicin, as it can potentially harm a developing baby. In premature babies and newborns, the drug is used with extra caution and careful dose monitoring. Children's doses are calculated based on body weight by the doctor.
